opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we've thought about quite a bit. There's a neat heuristic: under fairly general conditions, you'd expect developers to spend roughly comparable amounts on training and inference, give or take a factor of a few.

The reason is that the two are partially substitutable. To reach a given level of capability on a task, you can train a bigger or longer-trained model, or you can take a somewhat weaker model and spend more at inference time: more sampling, longer chains of reasoning, best-of-n with a verifier, search, that sort of thing. Across a bunch of domains, roughly an order of magnitude more training compute can be traded for something like an order of magnitude or so of inference compute, sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the task.

If that tradeoff holds and the returns look roughly symmetric on a log scale, the cost-minimizing allocation ends up with similar orders of magnitude on each side. If you were wildly lopsided, say spending a hundred times more on training than inference, you could probably shave a bit off training, add some test-time compute, and get the same performance more cheaply, and vice versa.

There are important caveats. First, training is a fixed cost amortized over every query, while inference scales with usage. So if you expect a huge deployment, a lot of tokens served, you want to push more into training, because a better or more efficient model pays off across all those queries. That's partly why labs overtrain smaller models relative to compute-optimal scaling. Second, the tradeoff isn't uniform. For tasks with cheap, reliable verification, like math or code with tests, inference scaling is very effective. For open-ended tasks it's much weaker. Third, latency and user experience constrain how much you can spend per query.

And there's a dynamic element. Inference-time scaling has really taken off with reasoning models, and reinforcement learning on reasoning blurs the line, since much of that "training" compute is really generating rollouts, which looks a lot like inference.

So my rough answer: don't expect one side to dominate by many orders of magnitude. A balanced allocation, roughly equal shares adjusted for deployment scale and how well your tasks benefit from test-time compute, is a good default, and that matches what we roughly see in the industry.

r001.rationale: The response says reallocating spending from a lopsided budget could preserve performance at lower cost. It does not clearly state that this reallocation can produce performance gains at unchanged total cost.

r002.rationale: It explicitly expects roughly comparable spending on training and inference and describes the efficient allocation as similar orders of magnitude.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the right way to think about this is that training and inference compute are, to a first approximation, substitutes. There's a tradeoff where you can spend more compute up front training a bigger or longer-trained model, and that gets you a certain level of capability, or you can spend less on training and then spend more at inference time—running more samples, doing more search, using longer chains of thought—and get to a similar level of performance. And some of the work we've done at Epoch suggests that the exchange rate between these is actually pretty favorable over certain ranges. You can get something like an order of magnitude reduction in training compute by spending maybe an order of magnitude more at inference, at least for some tasks.

So then the question of how you should divide spending becomes an economic one, and it depends a lot on how much demand there is for the model. If you're going to serve a model to hundreds of millions of users, then the inference cost is amortized over an enormous number of queries, and it makes sense to push much harder on training, because every bit of efficiency you squeeze into the model pays off across all of those queries. Whereas if you have a small number of very high-value tasks—say, you're trying to solve a particular hard math problem or do some kind of research—then it makes a lot more sense to just throw inference compute at the problem and not bother retraining.

What I think has been underappreciated until fairly recently is that the inference side has a lot more headroom than people assumed. For a long time the industry was very focused on scaling pretraining, and inference was treated as something you minimize. Now with reasoning models, the picture is that inference-time scaling is itself a dimension you can push on, and it has its own scaling laws. So I'd expect that over time a larger fraction of total compute spending shifts toward inference, partly because the demand side is growing—more users, more agents running for longer—and partly because the techniques for converting inference compute into capability have gotten a lot better.

But I'd add one caveat, which is that these aren't fully independent. A lot of the value of inference scaling comes from having a good base model to scale, and training is also increasingly spending compute on things like reinforcement learning that make the model better at using inference compute. So the clean split between the two is starting to blur, and I think the frontier labs are really optimizing over the whole pipeline rather than treating it as a fixed budget to divide.

r001.rationale: The response describes trading more inference compute for less training compute to reach similar performance, but does not say this can improve performance at unchanged total cost by shifting spending toward the smaller component.

r002.rationale: It discusses an approximately tenfold exchange between training and inference compute and predicts a larger inference share, but does not expect efficient training and inference spending to be of the same order of magnitude.

astra-6.text:
I think the right way to think about this is to optimize training and inference jointly. Spending more on training can give you a more capable model, but it can also let you achieve a given level of performance with a smaller model that’s cheaper to run. Whether that investment is worthwhile depends on how much you expect to use the model.

If you’re going to serve billions of queries, even a small reduction in the cost per query can justify a substantial increase in training expenditure. That pushes you toward training smaller models on more data than you would if you were just trying to get the best performance for a fixed training budget. If the model will see relatively little use, that additional training may not pay for itself.

There’s also the option of spending more compute at inference time to improve the quality of an answer. So you have to consider the task, the value of better answers, and constraints like latency. I don’t think there’s a universal percentage that should go to each. The question is where an additional dollar buys the most useful performance over the model’s lifetime.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing training and inference and how extra training can reduce per-query costs, but it does not say that a highly lopsided budget can improve performance at unchanged total cost by shifting spending to the smaller component.

r002.rationale: The response rejects a universal allocation but does not state or imply that efficient training and inference spending should be of the same order of magnitude.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to approach this is to ask: where does an additional dollar of compute produce the most value? Training is an upfront investment that can improve the model for every subsequent user. Inference is a cost you incur each time you use it, and spending more there can let the model work longer on a particular problem.

So the optimal split depends quite a lot on how much the model will be used. If you expect enormous demand, improvements from training get spread across many interactions, which makes that investment more attractive. If you’re tackling a smaller number of very valuable, difficult problems, it may make sense to spend much more compute at inference time.

Those choices also interact: you can train a model to make better use of additional inference compute. So I wouldn’t prescribe a fixed percentage. You want to jointly choose the training investment and the compute you spend per task, given demand, the value of better answers, and constraints like latency.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing training and inference spending based on demand and task value, but does not say that reallocating spend toward the smaller component can improve performance at unchanged total cost.

r002.rationale: The response rejects a fixed percentage but does not say efficient training and inference spending should be of the same order of magnitude.
